title: A Question of Antidotes
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 6 of 40
content:
The sixth hidden phial tried to bite me.

Not metaphorically.

The moment I broke the outer seal, the potion rose from the glass in a narrow red strand, formed something remarkably like a mouth, and snapped at the silver testing spoon.

I jerked my hand back.

Snape did not.

His wand moved once.

The red strand froze in midair, shivered, and dropped back into the phial.

“Impressive,” I said.

“Careless.”

“I meant the potion.”

“So did I.”

I looked at him.

He had already turned away, reaching for a containment bell.

“Did you know it would do that?”

“No.”

“You don't sound surprised.”

“I have found surprise to be of limited practical value.”

“That explains your parties.”

“I do not attend parties.”

“That explains them even more.”

The corner of his mouth threatened movement.

He placed the glass bell over the phial and sealed it with three flicks of his wand. The potion struck the inside of the dome once, then settled.

“Blood-reactive,” he said.

“I didn't cut myself.”

“No, but you handled the bitterroot earlier.”

I looked at my fingertips. “Trace residue?”

“Possibly.”

“That is extraordinarily sensitive.”

“It was designed to be.”

“For what?”

His expression changed.

There were moments when Snape became so still that I could almost see the decision happening behind his eyes: how much truth, how much omission, how much protection.

“Interrogation,” he said.

The word landed heavily.

“The draught was intended to react to elevated pulse and blood chemistry. Fear, pain, exertion. It would alter color when a subject became sufficiently distressed.”

“A lie detector?”

“A crude one.”

“Voldemort wanted it?”

“One of his lieutenants did. The Dark Lord approved.”

I looked at the phial.

“What did you do to it?”

Snape's gaze sharpened.

“You assume I did something.”

“The other five were sabotaged.”

“Patterns can encourage laziness.”

“So can evasiveness.”

He ignored that.

I ran the residual magic reader along the bell. It chimed twice, then shrieked.

“Interesting.”

“Move.”

Snape reached past me.

I caught his wrist before his fingers touched the bell.

We both froze.

Rule: no touching without warning unless someone was falling.

Apparently I had discovered an amendment for someone about to touch a blood-reactive potion.

His skin was cool. His pulse was not.

“Don't,” I said.

His eyes dropped to my hand.

I released him at once.

“What did the reader show?” he asked.

“Two layers. One old, one recent.”

“Recent?”

“Within months.”

“That is impossible.”

“Why?”

“Because I brewed it years ago.”

We looked at each other.

Then at the phial.

Someone had tampered with it after Snape.

The room changed around us.

Until then, the audit had been archaeology. Dangerous archaeology, but still the sorting of a finished war.

Now the past had a fresh fingerprint.

Snape drew his wand.

This time I did too.

“Who had access?” I asked.

“During the last school year? The Carrows. Selected Death Eaters. Anyone Voldemort chose to send.”

“After the battle?”

“Ministry evidence teams.”

“Reconstruction staff?”

“Not to the sealed stores.”

I thought of the wax. The official stamps. The careless question mark on the cabinet.

“Unless someone broke a seal and replaced it.”

Snape's face became unpleasantly focused.

“Your instrument.”

I handed it to him.

He scanned the phial, then the crate, then the shelf where we had found it. The needle quivered near the back wall.

“Again,” he said.

I joined him.

We moved every jar.

Behind the shelf was a narrow crack in the stone.

Snape pressed his wand tip against it and whispered a spell I did not recognize.

The mortar glowed green.

“Concealment charm,” he said.

“Yours?”

“No.”

The wall opened.

Inside was a cavity no larger than a bread box.

It held four more phials.

None were his.

I knew because he swore.

It was the first time I had heard him do it.

Not loudly. Not creatively. But with enough feeling that I almost laughed before remembering what we were looking at.

Each phial bore a thin silver mark etched into the glass: a hooked A.

“Alecto?” I asked.

His jaw tightened.

“Possibly.”

“What's in them?”

“I do not know.”

The admission came reluctantly.

I liked it more than I should have.

Snape was frightening when he knew everything in a room. There was something unexpectedly reassuring about hearing him say he did not.

“Then we find out,” I said.

“No.”

I blinked.

“No?”

“You will find out from behind a shield.”

“And you?”

“I will handle the samples.”

“You're still recovering from venom and nerve damage.”

“I am also more familiar with Dark potions than you are.”

“That does not make you poison-proof.”

“It does make me less likely to kill us through ignorance.”

I folded my arms.

He gave me a look that had probably terrorized adolescents for decades.

It did not improve with age.

“No,” I said.

His voice dropped. “This is not a negotiation.”

“Everything between adults is a negotiation unless someone is using force.”

His expression changed at that.

I continued before he could decide whether to be angry.

“We work together. You identify likely hazards. I handle precision work when your hand tires. We both stay behind the shield whenever the phials are open.”

“I do not require assistance.”

“You nearly dropped a memory two days ago.”

His face went white with anger.

I regretted the cruelty immediately, but not the point.

“I'm not saying you're incapable,” I said. “I'm saying your body is still healing, and pretending otherwise does not make you safer. It makes you easier to kill.”

Silence.

His gaze went to the hidden compartment.

When he spoke, the anger had become something colder.

“I have been easy to kill for some time.”

“No,” I said. “You've been willing to die. That's different.”

His eyes snapped to mine.

The words had come too fast to soften.

I could have apologized.

I did not.

For once, I wanted him to hear me without escape.

His throat worked.

“Do not presume—”

“I don't presume anything about why. I'm looking at the formula you wrote. Seven days of tissue saturation. Multiple neutralizers. A warning not to rely on it alone. You prepared to survive and then behaved as if survival was an administrative error.”

His face was unreadable.

Mine probably wasn't.

“That is not professional analysis,” he said.

“No.”

“What is it?”

I had no safe answer.

Concern sounded too intimate.

Frustration sounded too small.

“I don't know yet,” I said.

For some reason, honesty unsettled him more than either would have.

He looked away first.

“Shield,” he said.

I exhaled.

“Together?”

“Yes.”

It was as close to surrender as Severus Snape seemed capable of giving.

The first of Alecto's phials contained a modified Befuddlement Draught with a pain catalyst. The second contained a corrosive suspension meant to scar without immediately disabling. The third was a concentration of something I had never seen outside restricted medical texts.

Snape recognized it.

“Stop.”

I froze.

He leaned close to the glass, eyes narrowing.

“Acromantula venom.”

“Stabilized?”

“Yes.”

“With what?”

He stared.

Then he smiled.

It was not a pleasant smile.

“Poorly.”

He pointed at a faint sediment along the bottom.

“The stabilizer is separating. Another month and this would have become inert.”

“Deliberate?”

“No. Incompetence.”

“You sound delighted.”

“I am capable of enjoying small mercies.”

“Particularly when they insult a Carrow.”

“Especially then.”

We documented everything.

By evening, we had enough evidence to prove that the hidden cache was not Snape's and that at least one potion had been altered recently.

McGonagall came down herself.

Her face hardened as she read the report.

“This goes to Kingsley tonight.”

Snape's expression shuttered at the Minister's name.

“He will require a statement,” she added.

“I have given statements.”

“You have given insults in the approximate shape of statements.”

“They were accurate.”

McGonagall looked at me.

I looked at the ceiling.

“I shall send an Auror tomorrow,” she said.

Snape's hand tightened on his cane.

“No.”

“Severus.”

“No Aurors in my laboratory.”

“It is not currently your laboratory.”

The words struck harder than she meant them to.

I saw it.

McGonagall saw it too.

Her mouth softened, but Snape had already turned away.

“Use my office,” I said.

Both of them looked at me.

“I don't have an office,” I clarified. “So we can invent one. Empty classroom, neutral ground, whatever makes everyone stop posturing long enough to exchange information.”

McGonagall's eyebrows rose.

Snape looked murderous.

“Tomorrow at ten,” she said.

Then she left before either of us could object.

I began packing instruments.

Snape said, “You have an extraordinary talent for making my life worse.”

“You were supposed to be dead. There's significant room for improvement.”

He stared at me.

Then, impossibly, he laughed.

It hurt him. He pressed a hand to his throat and scowled as if the pain were my fault.

I smiled anyway.

On the table between us, the blood-reactive potion snapped once more at the glass.

The past was not finished.

Neither, apparently, was he.
